takeaway: Raised temperature, PCO2, H+ and 2,3-DPG shift the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, which means lower haemoglobin affinity for oxygen.

question.text: Which one of the following conditions results in decreased affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen?

lines.text: Here is the oxygen dissociation curve, and one condition that lowers affinity.
When the temperature rises, our red cell sweats and lets go of its oxygen balloons.
On the graph, the curve slides to the right. That is a right shift.
A right shift means a lower affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, so oxygen is released to the tissues more easily.
Other helpers push the curve the same way: a high carbon dioxide level, and a high hydrogen ion level, which together are the Bohr effect.
A high level of 2,3-DPG in the red cells shifts it right too.
So the answer is an increased temperature. Lower PCO2, fewer hydrogen ions or less 2,3-DPG all shift the curve left instead.
